DIDNTGOWELL:
Prenatal - I was really pressured to be induced. I also was a gestational diabetic and that was very hard at times.
Childbirth - Can't think of anything at the moment.
Postpartum - Breastfeeding support. Our baby's pediatrician said that our baby had a tongue tie at one of the first few visits, but the lactation consultant disagreed with her. Fast forward to 2 months later, I was having a lot of breastfeeding issues (VERY sore/bleeding nipples) and my baby was spitting up an abnormal amount of breastmilk on a daily basis. We finally got the referral to a pediatric dentist when my baby was about 3 months old. After his examination, he stated that she had severe oral ties (tongue, lip, and both cheeks). All were released at the visit that day. Overall, things did get better with breastfeeding in time. My breastfeeding journey was overall very challenging and I wish I could have received better support. I also got mastitis a few times postpartum, which was very challenging as well.

DIDNTGOWELL:
Prenatal:
The first midwife I saw after graduating from my fertility clinic made a comment that IVF patients are "high maintenance" and told me I probably caused a c section last time because I asked for an epidural too early. 

I ended up with a kidney stone in my third trimester. The first two times I visited OB triage at my delivery hospital, I had the same dismissive doctor who discharged me from my first birth (c-section) with inadequate pain management. I was not diagnosed until I came back a third time and had an absolute miracle doctor who really listened to me. I am not one to distrust my medical providers, so my issue with this doctor is very unusual for me. 

I was also caught between MFM, who wanted me induced by 39 weeks, and my delivery hospital, who has providers with wildly different willingness to offer inductions. After a ton of back and forth between the two practices, who don't talk to each other, it took a mental health provider from MFM calling someone she knew personally at the hospital, who suddenly allowed me to schedule induction. It was crazy to have to be the one relaying what MFM recommended as the patient.

Postpartum, I have grade II bladder prolapse. It hasn't gotten better with pelvic floor therapy, which my insurance stopped covering, and I have no idea what to expect or if I'll ever feel normal again.

I received a lot of conflicting information from my doctor and other providers about my daughter’s lip tie. 
She is a terrible sleeper so we were and still are very tired!

WENTWELL: When I switched from a regular OB to a midwife, I was much happier about my care. I felt heard and truly cared for by my midwife, but did not by the OB I started my first two visits with. My midwife looked for the root issues with my blood clotting and low platelets issues, and she worked to help me take the proper supplements to care for the situation in preparation for delivery, versus the OB who was just going to give me unhealthy shots in the weeks leading to delivery. I also received the best childbirth education and labor techniques than I had ever had with this baby #7! I wished I would have had this experience every time because I had never been more comfortable and confident during labor. In fact, at 8 cm when I entered the hospital, I was smiling and laughing between contractions and was handling labor greatly. Very shortly after entering the hospital, my water broke on its own and my baby was born about an hour later which I considered to be the only tough part of my 39 hour labor! One hour and I still handled well and was completely in control and managing pain well with the help of my husband and doula. I believe I only experienced this because of the education and supplements/health suggestions of my midwife’s care and because she recommended transferring me to a hospital that respects mother’s requests and rights. If I did not receive the care with my midwife, I may have experienced another horrible labor with a dangerous hemorrhage.

I had a lot of student drs taking care of me, never again. I had an epidural that I didn't want. A section I didn't want at 3 in the morning. The original epidural didn't take fully and I needed a repeat. So I received a second epidural in the OR. They proceeded with the C-section and then I began to throw up as I do not tolerate anesthesia well. I vomited 4 times while they were taking my baby out of me. They did place him on my chest for skin to skin until I vomited again. My after care was very nice.

My prenatal and labor care were great.  I had a good time and felt really well taken care of.  I do wish more attention and care is given to postpartum care though.  I've heard that in Korea they have postpartum centers were new moms can stay with their newborns for a couple of weeks after giving birth.  The moms are given time to rest from labor and delivery with professionals watching the newborns and giving them proper care.  At these centers, they're provided with nice rooms, great food (that's specially planned for recovering and nursing mothers), and information on how to take care of their babies.  They have classes where they can learn about everyday basics like giving the baby a bath, how to swaddle, etc.  Also they get to spend time with other new moms and share their experiences.  

I really wish they had centers like that in the US too.  I did some research on it while I was pregnant and I think there's only 1-2 cities in the US that have postpartum care centers and it's really a pity because I think there's a real need of it here in the US.

WENTWELL: I had an amazing, caring doctor. I researched extensively before deciding on seeing him. He listened super well to my concerns and I felt like we were a team. He made sure to address any concerns I had which helped ease my worries. During birth, I was equally blessed with an amazing team. My doctor made sure to speak to my nurse before my induction to catch her up to speed on our plan. My nurse was also very caring and went out of her way to make sure I was as mentally and physically comfortable as possible and checked on me and my baby consistently. My anesthesiologist was so so so kind and caring. I had had excruciating and traumatic births previously (even with epidurals) and he made sure to really listen to my previous experiences and asked several questions before starting to try to figure out why I had had problems with epidurals beforehand and he said “you’re not gonna be in pain, not on my watch” which was incredibly comforting. He was so gentle with the epidural placement and again went above and beyond to make sure it actually worked and that I was pain free throughout my birth. He even came to chat after the birth just to ask more questions and to make sure I had been satisfied with the care he provided. Everyone was very respectful of my wishes and concerns and overall it was a beautiful, gentle birth.  Postpartum team was great as well. They constantly checked on us and made sure we had everything we needed to be comfortable. I left the hospital with plenty of information and resources

DIDNTGOWELL:
I have had to advocate SO MUCH for all the support we have received. We are fortunate to be in a financial position where I have a flexible schedule, we have private insurance, access to IHS services, and can pay out of pocket when necessary. I have had to use EVERY resource to make sure my son gets the care he needs. 

I was most frustrated by the lack of breastfeeding support that I’ve received. I’ve paid out of pocket for craniosacral therapy and speech Language pathology evaluations because his pediatricians to find out why he is not drinking as much milk as other babies his age to support healthy weight gain. I’ve been vocal that my goal is to breastfeed 2+ years, but it seems that unless I switch to formula, IHS providers are not willing to provide support. 

I also went to the same IHS facility for myself to see why I was having a burning sensation in my urethra postpartum, and I was pressured to check for HIV and other STDs despite having already done at that during the pregnancy. Fortunately that issue went away on its own because those tests all came back negative (as expected), and no follow up was done to see what was actually causing the problem.

WENTWELL:
I have had to overcome a lot of challenges, but I am happy that I have had the support to continue nursing at 6 months in addition to introducing solid foods. My prenatal care mostly went well, but I switched providers 3 times to find one that matched my beliefs. 

I loved my doula. I specifically searched for a Native American doula in my area, and she was so supportive. I wish I had called her sooner during labor, but I was attempting to wait until I got through early labor, not knowing how quickly things would escalate with the Pitocin. 

My midwife provided a lot of helpful care from when I started seeing her in the 2nd trimester to when I risked out of her care at 38.5 weeks. She was much more focused on nutrition and physical preparation than pills.

DIDNTGOWELL: Not going into spontaneous labor on my own. I had to be induced - take a small pill. When I was at the hospital, I was 4cm and 80% dilated. I was getting there on my own, but they made me take a pill and do a balloon bag. The balloon bag thing never fell out so I thought I was always 4cm. I made them take it out after several hours bc it was uncomfortable, I was bleeding, and I was wet. They didn't want me to remove it bc they knew I was headstrong about intervention and they told me if they took it out, next steps would be Pitocin (they also said it would be days before I gave birth. HA!). Anyway, I had them take out the balloon finally and they completely disappeared and left me alone. I didn't totally hate it but I didn't realize I was in active labor and when my body started pushing and ejecting the baby, I had no idea bc in my mind I was barely 4cm and it was going to take days! Anyway, my doula finally got there and took one look at me and ran into the hallway and got someone to check me and they said, I see the baby, baby is coming. The rest is history. Moral of the story - health care providers did not entertain that everyone is different and that an unmedicated vaginal birth can be done in a hospital.

She eggs on my cosleeping and parenting styles. My partner (traditionally native ceremony married just not colonizer federally legal married) is amazing and supportive. I have all the care I need through native health services family practitioner.
